title: My Open Data
html:
Over the past few years, it has been great to witness and experience the push for more and more open data practices by public institutions especially humanitarian-related ones.  There is still a long way to go, but the trend is moving in the right direction.

But, what struck me a couple weeks ago was that as an advocate of open data, I do not have any of my personal (not private) data “open”. The  question that came to my mind was: Can I really be an open data advocate if I do not even share some of my personal data openly? So, I figured that I should should start figuring out how to share some of it.

As Robert Scoble points out, with the spread of new wearable tech gadgets and a variety of sensors combined with loyalty programs, companies will soon know a lot about us. Some companies already have a lot of data and know a lot about us. Target, for example, has a 50+ person strong data and analysis branch that can often determine, with a high degree of accuracy, if someone in your household is pregnant before that person even announces it. And, they do this with their loyalty program data. Others actively collect information and then sell it (e.g. Rapleaf and InfiniGraph).  With the spread of wearable tech and senors, knowing this kind of information will become ever more important for companies to compete and survive. And that data will need to be presented to their senior management, in live time, on mobile devices.

Enough about companies though. What about us as individuals?  As these devices become more prevalent, they will allow us to easily collect and store data in a structured ways. There is becoming a huge increase in personal data available and a large amount that we can share (if we choose). But are we setup as individuals to track our data in a consolidated way and then share that data? I don’t think so. Partly because we have not been thinking this way (I am not familiar with any services catering to individuals rather than companies) and most people are concerned about their privacy.

The interesting question for me becomes: There are many firms out there collecting data about us, our movements, and our activities online.  They are gaining a lot of knowledge about us. So, why can’t I know the same thing about myself as they know?

In an initial, small step, I have started putting together some of my more structured data into Google spreadsheets and then linking them to My Open Data page.  The data that I am opening are:

1) Books: the books I have finished and the ones that I hope to read. Quite often I have been asked for a list of the books that I have been reading. I track them in a Google spreadsheet and share it when asked.  Why not Amazon or Goodreads? Because these services never seem to cover all the books that I am interested in. So, as a tech-lover, I created my own spreadsheet so that I could have complete control.  The data.

2) Swimming - I swim on a very regular basis. I swam competitively as a kid and got back into it for exercise a couple years ago. In December 2012, I bought a Swimovate watch and started tracking my outings (The data). I also started tracking where I swim - the map  and related data.

3) Body Weight: how my body weight is changing over time. (The data)

I am also looking at adding other data sets (e.g. structured feed of all my Twitter messages). As I sort them out, I will add them to my My Open Data page for anyone to find.

I would be quite interested to hear your thoughts about the concepts above so feel free to leave a comment below.

Andrej
